newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major says not bargaining with IRA guerrillas.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major says not bargaining with IRA guerrillas.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major said on Thursday he would not bargain with the Irish Republican Army (IRA) over a ceasefire to allow the guerrillas' political wing Sinn Fein to take part in Northern Irish peace talks.
Sinn Fein immediately accused Major of bowing to pressure from pro-British Protestant Unionists in Northern Ireland and of setting back the peace process.
The president of Sinn Fein, Gerry Adams, accused the British prime minister of sabotaging his efforts to reach a settlement with moderate Irish nationalist John Hume.
"No matter how positively or softly Mr Major's statement is interpreted, there is no doubt it is a rejection of our initiative," Adams said.
The Dublin government gave an equally frosty response. Prime Minister John Bruton said: "It is better to wait before you have reached agreement before publishing preliminary points of view".
But Major appeared to hold open the possibility of a swift entry into the peace talks for Sinn Fein, if the Irish Republican Army declares a Christmas truce.
Major told parliament: "The talks that have been carrying on for some time are likely to break for Christmas soon and to resume later in January."

"When Sinn Fein can join the talks depends upon their own actions. We need to see an unequivocal restoration of the ceasefire. We need to be able to make a credible judgment that it's lasting...We are not seeking delay."
Major, saying he wanted to dispel rumours, clarified the terms on which Sinn Fein could enter the peace talks from which they have been barred.

Major's remarks -- which were backed up by a detailed written statement -- followed attempts by Hume, the leader of the Catholic nationalist SDLP party, to break the deadlock over Sinn Fein's participation in peace talks.
In the written statement, the government said Hume had suggested a new IRA ceasefire was available if Britain clarified its position on various issues.
These included the length of the multi-party peace talks, the scrapping of guerrilla arms and ways of building confidence in the British-ruled province.
Major told a television interviewer later: "What we have done is set out what our policy is. I hope...they will now respond with a ceasefire that will need to be credible."
The IRA abandoned a 17-month ceasefire in February with a series of bombings on the British mainland.

But the guerrillas have not carried out any attacks for nearly two months since an attack on an army base in Northern Ireland killed one soldier, raising speculation that they are operating an unofficial truce to win concessions for Sinn Fein.
Many politicians believe that if progress is not made by the end of the year, the whole process will be put on ice for several months as Britain concentrates on the coming election.

Sinn Fein chairman Mitchel McLaughlin told the British Broadcasting Company (BBC): "It is a step back, unquestionably a step back...John Major has reneged on his commitment to the Irish peace process."
Hume, who said he was surprised by Major's statement, said he would be seeking a meeting with Major, adding he thought a restoration of the IRA ceasefire was achievable.

Pro-British Unionists, who had been pressurising Major to publish his response to the Hume proposals to dispel their fears that Britain had been doing secret deals with the republicans, were pleased by Thursday's statement.

Ulster Unionist leader David Trimble said: "What I interpret this as meaning is that the government is determined not to be taken in by some purely tactical exercise like the one the IRA ran in the last couple of years."
